prop: Every observation in this memo was taken against the tetel worktree at commit c821b94d6e1fbf4dc43a1691c975e440448534d2 on branch tet30-prose-revised-since-proof, with a clean working tree.

The `prose-revised-since-proof` listing is a pure function of three recomputed quantities and stores none of them: a block's current (text, cite-list) pair, the timestamp at which that exact pair first appeared in the block's event history, and an anchor equal to the maximum over the block's cited claims of each claim's earliest non-refuting record whose proposition digest matches the claim's current wording. The block is listed exactly when the pair's first-appearance timestamp exceeds the anchor, and is skipped outright when it is a heading, when its current cite-list is empty, or when no cited claim has such a record.

The acknowledgement event cannot live in `prose.jsonl`. `ProseEvent` is an internally-tagged serde enum over exactly `Create` and `Revise`, and `workspace::read_jsonl` propagates any line's parse failure as an error over the whole log rather than skipping it; empirically, a build at this pin reading a `prose.jsonl` containing one valid `Create` line and one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line fails the entire read with `unknown variant \`Ack\`, expected \`Create\` or \`Revise\`` and exits 1. A new tag value therefore makes every older build unable to read even the prose it already understood.

A sibling `acks.jsonl`, added to `snapshot::SNAPSHOT_FILES`, degrades safely in the older build it will be shipped past: that constant is an explicit enumeration whose stated purpose is that a future workspace file be a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, so a build that predates the entry simply never opens the file, reads `prose.jsonl` unchanged, and reproduces TET-30's un-suppressed listing. The failure direction is therefore over-reporting a residue entry a newer build would suppress, never suppressing one an older build would show.

For a claims-unaffected prose edit — a typo or wording fix that leaves every cited claim's proposition untouched — both of TET-30's two clearing acts misrepresent what the author did. Restoring the text and citation list, which C6 names as the first act, restores the defect the edit corrected. Revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded, C6's second act, requires changing a claim that is correct; and because `out_of_proof` is one of the disjuncts of `Findings::machine_check_failed` while `prose_revised_since_proof` is not, that route drives the run to a machine failure until a further grounding pass lands, spending a red check and a pass to silence a line that never failed the run.

An acknowledged block must still print, not vanish. Deleting the entry would make "no post-proof prose revision exists in this memo" and "one exists and a human has read it against its claims" indistinguishable in the check report, whereas this crate treats distinguishable states as owed distinct output — its no-rows path says so in as many words, that being "a distinct state from a clean run, not a weaker way of spelling it". Printing also costs nothing the residue does not already pay: the entry format already carries an author's own `--why` verbatim under `revised because:`, with the source comment stating that it is never a paraphrase and is the most actionable thing the entry can hand a reader.

An acknowledged block should leave the `prose-revised-since-proof` group and be printed instead under one collapsed document-level bullet carrying, per acknowledged block, its id, its document line, its acknowledgement timestamp and the author's `--why` verbatim. This is the shape the crate already reaches for: the residue's own preamble is one document-level bullet, and the comment justifying it names `ledger_has_no_scope_columns` as precedent on the ground that a constant repeated per row buries the findings that are about this document. Leaving the block inside the demanding group with an extra annotation would keep a standing demand a human has already discharged, which is the skim-training failure the design exists to remove; removing it from the report entirely is refused by the preceding claim.

The acknowledgement is an event in `acks.jsonl` recording five things — the block id, the block's current text, its current citation list, the sha256 digest of each cited claim's proposition as it stands at ack time, and a verbatim `--why` — plus the `workspace::now_unix()` timestamp every workspace event carries. A listing is suppressed if and only if some ack for that block records a text, citation list and set of cited-claim proposition digests all equal, byte for byte, to the ones the check recomputes for that block at check time. The predicate is pure equality over recomputed values; nothing derived is stored, and the recorded digests are exactly the `sha256_hex(claim.proposition)` values `prose_after_proof` already computes for its in-proof test.

The sketch's second suppression clause — that the ack's timestamp be later than the recomputed anchor — is dropped, because it cannot fire. The rule is only consulted for a block the trigger already listed, and listing means the current pair's first-appearance timestamp already exceeds the anchor; an ack recording that same current pair is appended to an append-only log by the same authoring workspace, after that pair exists, and stamped by the same `workspace::now_unix()` that stamped the prose event. So unless the authoring machine's clock runs backwards between the two appends, the ack's timestamp exceeds the block timestamp which already exceeds the anchor, and the clause is satisfied in every case it is evaluated. Dropping it leaves the suppression predicate free of any timestamp comparison at all, which is why — unlike the trigger it guards — the acknowledgement does not rest on two clocks agreeing.

Three invalidation invariants follow from the key, each with the mutation that reddens its test. (i) Any later change to the block's text or to its citation list voids the ack, because both are components of the key; the mutation is to compare only the text, after which a citation-only revision — which TET-30's C6 records as an act that lists rather than clears — would stay suppressed. (ii) Any change to a cited claim's proposition voids the ack, because the key carries that claim's proposition digest; the mutation is to drop the digest set from the key, after which an ack would outlive a rewrite of the very claim the author read the paragraph against. (iii) A workspace with no `acks.jsonl` produces byte-identical output to today's, because `workspace::read_jsonl` treats a missing file as an empty log rather than an error; the mutation is to make the missing file an error, after which every memo rendered before this design existed would fail to check.

The acknowledgement is a strict filter over the trigger's output, applied after `prose_after_proof` has produced its list, and therefore cannot add a listing that TET-30 would not have produced — a stale, malformed or unmatched ack simply fails to suppress, which is the same state as no ack at all. Two consequences hold without further argument: the set of blocks the reader is asked to act on is always a subset of TET-30's, so no new false demand can be manufactured; and `machine_check_failed` is untouched, since `prose_revised_since_proof` is not among its disjuncts and the ack changes only which entries populate it. It also follows that the digest component does not close any part of TET-30's conceded non-coverage for prose that ships alongside a claim revision — it only stops an acknowledgement outliving the state it attested to.

The acknowledgement is an event in `acks.jsonl` recording five things — the block id, the block's current text, its current citation list, the sha256 digest of each cited claim's proposition **as `claims.jsonl` holds it**, and a verbatim `--why` — plus the `workspace::now_unix()` timestamp every workspace event carries. A listing is suppressed if and only if some ack for that block records a text, citation list and set of cited-claim proposition digests all equal, byte for byte, to the ones the check recomputes for that block at check time, with the digests recomputed from the snapshot's `claims.jsonl` — the same source the ack was minted from, and deliberately not the ledger-derived propositions the in-proof test must use, since the two are not the same string and a claim whose proposition carries an embedded newline or edge whitespace would otherwise be unackable with nothing red to say so. The predicate is pure equality over recomputed values; nothing derived is stored.
why: F8: the trigger's in-proof digests are computed over ledger-derived propositions, which differ from claims.jsonl's by newline replacement and cell trimming. An ack minted in the workspace can only see claims.jsonl, so a key stated as "the digest the trigger computes" would never match for a claim with an embedded newline or edge whitespace, and would do so silently. The key must name its digest source explicitly and use the same source on both sides.

prop: The minting surface is one verb, `tetel prose --ack <id> --why <text>` with the matching MCP argument pair, built as a variant of the single request shape both front ends already share so the two cannot drift on which missing flag is refused. Its refusals are exactly the workspace-decidable ones the existing prose verbs use, raised through the same `workspace::refuse` helper: no such block, the block is a heading, the block carries no citations, a cited id that does not resolve to a claim in `claims.jsonl`, and an empty `--why` — the last on the identical `why.trim().is_empty()` test that already backs "--revise requires --why (revisions must explain themselves)". None inspects the content or plausibility of the reason. The verb cannot refuse an ack on a block that is not currently listed, because an authoring workspace holds no evidence records at all — they live beside the rendered memo — so it cannot compute an anchor; and it need not, since an ack on an unlisted block suppresses nothing.

An acknowledgement must not enter `render`'s output. Keeping the rendered bytes a function of facts, claims, prose, targets and transplants only — with `acks.jsonl` shipped by the snapshot copy loop but never read by `compose::render` — preserves the determinism the provenance-drift finding rests on, and buys a property that makes the required re-render honest rather than merely tolerable: re-rendering after an ack and nothing else rewrites the snapshot in place, since existing snapshot files are overwritten, while leaving the memo byte-identical. The discharge therefore shows up in version control as a change to the record and no change to the argument, which is exactly what it is.

Supersession needs no verb and withdrawal needs one, and both are resolved by log order rather than by timestamp. Supersession is automatic: since suppression is existential over matching keys, a later ack with a different key simply fails to match and a duplicate ack for the same key changes nothing. Withdrawal is a second event, `Unack`, carrying a block id and its own required verbatim `--why`; suppression then requires a key-matching ack appended after the last `Unack` for that block. Naming only the block, rather than a key, is sufficient because a key-mismatched ack is already void. Resolving by position in an append-only log written one line per event, rather than by comparing timestamps, keeps the whole acknowledgement mechanism free of clock comparisons. Withdrawal has to exist: without it, an author who acknowledged in error and cannot yet rewrite the paragraph would have no honest act available — which is precisely the defect this design was written to remove, reproduced one level up.

The implementation surface is four declared modification targets plus a new `acks` module, and the censuses bound the blast radius. `prose_after_proof` gains an acks input and returns the listed and acknowledged partitions rather than one list; it has exactly one production call site, in `lib.rs`, the other 31 occurrences being its own definition, eighteen unit-test calls in `checks.rs` and doc-comment or test-name references. `prose_revised_since_proof` on `Findings` gains a sibling field for the acknowledged partition, touching five sites in three files. `SNAPSHOT_FILES` grows from nine entries to ten, touching one file. `NON_COVERAGE` gains entries, touching one file. No other symbol in the worktree needs to change.

This design knowingly breaks both halves of TET-30's C11 sentence "Nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes": a tenth file ships, and a new event schema exists. The price is bounded and should be stated rather than absorbed. `check` always prints the binary that produced a report, on the stated ground that a report which does not name its build cannot be disbelieved, so two reports disagreeing about one memo's residue can be attributed to their checkers — which is sufficient for the only divergence this change can produce, an older build over-reporting an entry a newer one suppresses. It is not sufficient to tell the reader of a single old report that an acknowledgement exists at all; what covers that is the acknowledgement log itself, which the snapshot ships beside the memo and which is readable without any tetel build.

Two entries are owed in `NON_COVERAGE`, by the list's own stated standard that a deliberate exclusion earns its own line because a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed. First: that an acknowledgement records only that a human said they re-read the paragraph against its claims, and that nothing verifies the reading happened or judges whether the paragraph is faithful — the tool's silence after an ack is the author's assertion, not the tool's finding. Second: that an acknowledgement minted after the last `render --out` is not in the snapshot the check reads, so it does not suppress anything until the memo is re-rendered. Both are static general statements, which is the only form entries in this constant can take.

Per-citation attribution is folded into the acknowledgement only as far as it honestly can be, which is not far. `NON_COVERAGE`'s last entry already states that whether a block's wording was ever examined against an earlier-settled co-citation is never answered by any listing, and the acknowledgement does not answer it either: the ack is per block, its key merely records every cited claim's digest, and the only place a per-citation judgement can appear is inside the author's verbatim `--why`, which the tool must not parse. The design's contribution is therefore to print the block's cited claim ids beside that verbatim reason in the acknowledged bullet, so a reader can pair the author's own words to the citations, and to leave the non-coverage entry standing.

The acknowledgement log is re-homeable into TET-36's obligation ledger without rewriting a single event, because no field in it is specific to this residue. It records a block id, the block's text and citation list, a digest per cited claim, a reason and a timestamp; it records none of the quantities `prose_after_proof` derives — not the anchor, not any claim's first proof, not the block timestamp, not whether the block was listed. A general ledger consuming these as discharge records for one obligation class therefore needs the events as they stand and a rule that reads them, which is a re-homing rather than a rework.

This design neither settles nor depends on TET-61's separate question of warning an author at `prose --revise` time. It changes only the economics of that question: today such a warning could name no act, since the workspace verbs are create and revise and neither discharges anything, whereas afterwards it could name the ack verb. Whether the warning is worth building remains a measurement question this memo does not answer.

why: F8 is the fact that forced this claim's digest-source clause, but the earlier revision changed only the proposition and left the citations at F2,F7 — so the clause about ledger-derived versus claims.jsonl propositions rested on evidence the claim did not cite. Adding F8.

prop: There is no withdrawal verb, and supersession needs none. Supersession is automatic: suppression is existential over matching keys, so a later ack with a different key fails to match and a duplicate ack for the same key changes nothing. Withdrawal was designed in and then removed, because a negative event is droppable in a way the ack's other invalidators are not: `snapshot::write` copies and never removes, so a snapshot's ack log is the most recent copy any build made of it rather than the workspace's log as of the last render, and a render by a build predating `acks.jsonl` refreshes `prose.jsonl` and `claims.jsonl` while leaving that file untouched. Every other condition that voids an ack — the block's text, its citation list, each cited claim's proposition — travels in files every build already ships and rewrites, so a stale ack log can only survive into a state it legitimately describes. An `Unack` would have been the single exception, and the state it protects against is not symmetric with the defect this design fixes: an author who acknowledged in error and now believes the paragraph is faulty has an honest and correct act available, namely repairing the paragraph, which voids the ack by changing its key.
why: F13 refutes the previous answer. `snapshot::write` copies and never removes, so a snapshot's ack log is the most recent copy any build ever made of it, not the workspace's log at last render. An `Unack` is therefore droppable — a render by a build that does not know `acks.jsonl` refreshes prose and claims and leaves the old ack file, and the ack it withdrew silently suppresses again. Every other ack-invalidating condition is carried by files every build already ships and refreshes; the withdrawal event was the only one that was not. Removing it is what makes a stale ack log unable to suppress anything it should not.

prop: A sibling `acks.jsonl` degrades in one direction only, but this needs two things rather than one. prop: A snapshot's `acks.jsonl` is not covered by provenance drift, and this design does not create that category but joins it. `compose::render` builds the memo from exactly five workspace logs — prose, claims, targets, transplants and facts — so of the nine files a snapshot ships, only those five are re-rendered and therefore only those five are drift-covered; `counters.json`, `pending.json`, `refusals.log` and `identity.json` are already shipped outside that coverage, and `identity.json` is already a file outside it that decides what the report says, namely whether a claim was self-grounded or independently grounded. why: C21 establishes a third owed entry — the snapshot ack log's absence from drift coverage (F15) — so "two entries are owed" is no longer the count this design implies.

why: Both graders hit this from opposite sides. The grounder: once C4's reconciliation lands, an `Unack` travels in the same rewritten log as every ack and is no more droppable, for any current build — so the droppability reason rested on a premise this memo elsewhere undertakes to falsify. The attacker: a duplicate ack changes nothing for suppression but leaves the output C7 mandates with two candidate reasons. The decision does not change, but its load-bearing reason does: the act-availability argument now leads, droppability is demoted to the downgrade-only case it actually covers.

prop: An acknowledged block should leave the `prose-revised-since-proof` group and be printed instead under one collapsed document-level bullet carrying, per acknowledged block, its id, its document line, its acknowledgement timestamp and the author's `--why` verbatim. Because `--why` and the timestamp are recorded but not part of the key, several acks can match one block's current key at once; the entry prints the EARLIEST such ack's reason and timestamp, mirroring the trigger's own use of the earliest event bearing the current pair, so that what a reader sees is the moment the discharge was first made rather than the most recent restatement of it. This collapsed shape is what the crate already reaches for: the residue's own preamble is one document-level bullet, and the comment justifying it names `ledger_has_no_scope_columns` as precedent on the ground that a constant repeated per row buries the findings that are about this document. Leaving the block inside the demanding group with an extra annotation would keep a standing demand a human has already discharged, which is the skim-training failure the design exists to remove; removing it from the report entirely is refused by the preceding claim.
why: Qualified: the ack's `--why` and timestamp are recorded but unkeyed, so an author acknowledging one unchanged block twice with different reasons leaves this bullet with two candidate reasons and two candidate timestamps and no stated selection rule. Adding the rule, and choosing the earliest to mirror the trigger's own min-keying over the pair.

prop: The minting surface is exactly one verb — there is no withdrawal verb — namely `tetel prose --ack <id> --why <text>` with the matching MCP argument pair, added as a variant of the single request shape both front ends share. That shared shape is necessary but not sufficient for the two front ends to agree, and this verb is the case that shows why: the ack carries no text, yet `ProseParams` declares `text: String` with neither `Option` nor `#[serde(default)]` while `Command::Prose` declares `text: Option<String>` with a stdin fallback, so an ack over MCP is refused by deserialisation before any `workspace::refuse` is reached while the same ack over the CLI is not. Making `text` optional on the MCP side is therefore part of this design, and it moves the existing create path's missing-text refusal out of the schema and into code that must state it. Separately, each front end selects its mode with an if/else-if chain that constructs one variant and silently discards whatever inputs that variant has no field for, so an ack combined with `--revise`, `--heading`, `--cites` or `--before` would drop one without a word — the same shape as the defect this crate already fixed once, and a refusal this design must add rather than inherit. Of the ack's five refusals only two are ones an existing prose verb already makes: a block that does not exist, and an empty `--why` on the identical `why.trim().is_empty()` test that backs "--revise requires --why (revisions must explain themselves)". Three are new gates, because prose creation is deliberately ungated: the block must not be a heading and must carry citations, since a listing exists for neither; and every cited id must resolve to a claim in `claims.jsonl`, because the ack's key is a digest per cited claim and an unresolvable id has none. None inspects the content or plausibility of the reason. The verb cannot refuse an ack on a block that is not currently listed, because an authoring workspace holds no evidence records at all — they live beside the rendered memo — so it cannot compute an anchor; and it need not, since an ack on an unlisted block suppresses nothing.
why: Qualified by F16: the shared request shape does not reach the layer the drift is on. `ProseParams.text` is schema-required while `Command::Prose.text` is optional with a stdin fallback, and the ack mode carries no text — so the MCP server refuses the verb before `workspace::refuse` is reached and the CLI does not. Each front end also selects its mode with an if/else-if chain that silently discards inputs its chosen arm has no field for. The claim's "so the two front ends cannot drift" was exactly wrong for this verb.

prop: The implementation surface is nine declared modification targets plus a new `acks` module. On the check side: `prose_after_proof` gains an acks input and returns the listed and acknowledged partitions rather than one list — of its 33 matching lines exactly one is a production call site, the other 32 being its definition, 18 unit-test calls, and doc-comment or test-name references; `prose_revised_since_proof` on `Findings` gains a sibling field, touching five sites in three files; `SNAPSHOT_FILES` grows from nine entries to ten, touching one file; `NON_COVERAGE` gains entries, touching one file; and `snapshot::write` must reconcile rather than accrete, a definition with exactly two callers, one per front end. On the authoring side the shared request shape is a surface rather than a shield, and it does not reach far enough on its own: `ProseRequest` is an enum consumed by an exhaustive match, so an ack mode adds a variant and an arm across its 13 matching lines in four files; `ProseOutcome` gains a variant across its 9 matching lines; and because the drift this verb exposes sits above that shape, `ProseParams` must relax its required `text` across its 2 matching lines and `Command::Prose` must gain the flag and a refusal for conflicting modes across its 1 relevant matching line. What the censuses establish is where each of these symbols is used today; that no further symbol needs to change is a judgement about code not yet written, and no census can settle it.
why: Qualified twice. The attacker: the target list omitted `ProseParams` and `Command::Prose`, both nameable today and neither visited by the `ProseRequest`/`ProseOutcome` censuses. The grounder: `ProseRequest` matches 13 lines, not 12. Both corrected; the list is now nine targets.

prop: Three invalidation invariants follow from the key, each with the mutation that reddens its test. (i) Any later change to the block's text or to its citation list voids the ack, because both are components of the key; the mutation is to compare only the text, after which a citation-only revision — which TET-30's C6 records as an act that lists rather than clears — would stay suppressed. (ii) Any change to a cited claim's proposition voids the ack, because the key carries that claim's proposition digest; the mutation is to drop the digest set from the key, after which an ack would outlive a rewrite of the very claim the author read the paragraph against. (iii) For a memo whose snapshot carries no `acks.jsonl` — which is every memo rendered before this design, and every memo whose author never acknowledged anything — the residue reports exactly the entries it reports today, because `workspace::read_jsonl` treats a missing file as an empty log rather than an error; the mutation is to make the missing file an error, after which every previously rendered memo would fail to check. Invariant (iii) is stated over the residue's own findings and not over the report's bytes, because this design also adds entries to `NON_COVERAGE`, which prints on every report and therefore changes the bytes of all of them. Its object is the snapshot rather than the workspace, because the snapshot is what the check reads.
why: Qualified: invariant (iii) was stated at byte level, and this memo's own C17 falsifies it — the non-coverage print loop is unconditional, so three new entries change the report text of every memo ever checked, including memos with no ack log. The invariant is restated over the residue's own findings, which is the level it was always about.

prop: Every source observation in this memo was taken against the tetel worktree at commit c821b94d6e1fbf4dc43a1691c975e440448534d2 on branch tet30-prose-revised-since-proof. The pin observation recorded at the head of this memo's evidence captured `git status --porcelain -b` printing only the branch line — no modified, staged or untracked path of any kind — and no tracked file was modified at any point thereafter. The paths this design has since added to the tree are its own output and nothing else: the rendered memo, its snapshot directory, and its evidence ledger, all three untracked, all three postdating every observation the memo rests on.
why: Qualified: `git status --porcelain -b` shows three untracked paths, not the two the sentence enumerated before closing with "both" — the evidence ledger is design output too. The claim now names all three and attributes the empty-status observation to the pin record that captured it rather than asserting a bare past instant.

prop: For a claims-unaffected prose edit — a typo or wording fix that leaves every cited claim's proposition untouched — neither clearing act TET-30 names represents what the author did, and the two differ in what they cost. Restoring the text and citation list, which TET-30's C6 names as the first act, restores the defect the edit corrected. The second act has two branches. Revising a cited claim requires changing a claim that is correct, and because `out_of_proof` is one of the disjuncts of `Findings::machine_check_failed` while `prose_revised_since_proof` is not, it drives the run to a machine failure until a further grounding pass lands — spending a red check and a pass to silence a line that never failed the run. Adding a citation to a newly minted claim changes no correct claim and reddens nothing, since an ungrounded claim is human-owed rather than a machine failure; it still requires inventing a claim the paragraph did not need and buying a grounding pass for it. Neither branch is a description of a typo fix.
why: Qualified: the disjunction "revising or adding" does not carry both consequents. Adding a citation to a newly minted claim changes no correct claim, and an ungrounded claim is human-owed rather than a machine failure — so that branch costs a grounding pass but never a red check. The claim now separates the two branches and states each cost exactly.

prop: A sibling `acks.jsonl` degrades in one direction only, and needs no change to `snapshot::write` to do it. Two properties give it. First, the manifest: `SNAPSHOT_FILES` is an explicit enumeration whose stated purpose is that a future workspace file be a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, so a build predating the entry never opens the file, reads `prose.jsonl` unchanged, and reproduces TET-30's un-suppressed listing. Second, monotonicity: `append_jsonl` only appends, no authoring verb deletes or truncates a workspace log — every `fs::remove` in `src/` is scratch-directory teardown in a test region, none of it in the modules holding the authoring verbs — and this design ships no withdrawal verb, so a workspace's ack log only grows. Together these mean a snapshot's ack log, however stale, is a prefix of the workspace's: it holds a subset of the acks, suppresses a subset of the blocks, and therefore over-reports rather than under-reports. An earlier draft of this design mandated that `snapshot::write` reconcile — deleting snapshot files absent from the workspace — to close a gap that monotonicity had already closed; that mandate is withdrawn, and with it the only irreversible cross-build behaviour the design contained, which would have let any build predating a future snapshot file destroy it on render.
why: F18 refutes the need for the reconciliation this claim mandated. With no withdrawal verb (C14) and no production removal path anywhere in src/, a workspace log is monotone, so a snapshot's copy is always a PREFIX of the current workspace log — fewer acks, therefore fewer suppressions, which is the over-reporting direction this claim already calls safe. Reconciliation addressed a case the no-withdrawal decision had already closed, while buying a permanently destructive change to a shared writer that would let any predating build delete a shipped log it does not understand — including, later, TET-36's. The mandate is struck and the one-directional property re-derived from monotonicity instead.

prop: The acknowledgement is a strict filter over the trigger's output, applied after `prose_after_proof` has produced its list, and therefore cannot add a listing that TET-30 would not have produced: the set of blocks the reader is asked to act on is always a subset of TET-30's, so no new false demand can be manufactured. A stale ack and an unmatched ack each simply fail to suppress, which is the same state as no ack at all. A malformed one is not the same, and the difference must be decided rather than assumed: `workspace::read_jsonl` propagates a bad line as an error over the whole log rather than degrading it to an empty one, and the silent `if let Ok(...)` the prose call site uses is defended there by a premise this design deliberately falsifies for acks — that a corrupt file already reddened provenance, which cannot happen for a log `compose::render` never reads. So an unreadable `acks.jsonl` in a snapshot must redden, joining the existing rule that "Drift and an unreadable snapshot are machine failures: both are objective contradictions between a document and the record it claims to rest on, decidable without a human." That is the one point at which this design touches `machine_check_failed`, and it touches it for corruption of the record, never for anything an acknowledgement means: no ack, however stale or unmatched, moves a claim between the machine and human-owed partitions.
why: Qualified: "stale, malformed or unmatched ... collapses to the same behaviour" is false for malformed. `workspace::read_jsonl` returns an error over the whole log rather than an empty one, and the `if let Ok(...)` swallow the prose call site uses is justified there by a premise — that a corrupt prose.jsonl already reddened provenance — which C13 and C21 deliberately make false for acks.jsonl. The claim now separates the three cases and states the reporting decision the third one owes.

prop: There is no withdrawal verb, and supersession needs none. Supersession is automatic for suppression: matching is existential over keys, so a later ack with a different key fails to match and a duplicate ack for the same key cannot change whether a block is suppressed. Withdrawal was designed in and then removed, and the reason that carries the decision is that the state it protects is not symmetric with the defect this design fixes: an author who acknowledged in error and now believes the paragraph is faulty has an honest and correct act available, namely repairing the paragraph, which voids the ack by changing its key — whereas TET-30's defect was precisely that a correct paragraph left its author no act at all. Declining to add the verb also keeps the ack log monotone, which is what makes a stale snapshot copy of it a prefix rather than an arbitrary earlier state, and so keeps the whole mechanism's failure direction one-way. An `Unack` would have broken that: a render by a build predating `acks.jsonl` leaves the log at whatever the last knowing render wrote, and a withdrawal appended after that render would vanish while the acknowledgement it cancelled survived — the one way a negative event could be lost while a positive one persisted.
why: C4's reconciliation mandate is withdrawn (F18), so this claim's closing sentence — which bounded the droppability hazard to "once this design's reconciliation lands" — refers to something the design no longer contains. The hazard is now bounded by monotonicity instead, which also makes the droppability consideration weaker still: a stale ack log is a prefix, so what a predating build's render actually loses is any event appended since, whether positive or negative.

prop: A sibling `acks.jsonl` degrades in one direction only, and gets there by three properties rather than two, the third of which this design must supply. First, the manifest: `SNAPSHOT_FILES` is an explicit enumeration whose stated purpose is that a future workspace file be a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, so a build predating the entry never opens the file, reads `prose.jsonl` unchanged, and reproduces TET-30's un-suppressed listing. Third, and this is what monotonicity alone does not give: the ack event must also record the identity of the workspace that minted it, and suppression must require that identity to equal the one in the snapshot's `identity.json`. Without it the one-directional property is false, because a memo is not bound to a renderer — `render --out` takes its workspace from a free global flag with no comparison against the existing snapshot — and `snapshot::write` skips a file the current workspace lacks instead of removing it. So rendering a memo from a second workspace that never held an ack leaves the first workspace's ack log beside the second's prose and claims: a superset of what any one workspace holds, silently suppressing a block the true state would list. With the identity component the stale log is voided by mismatch rather than honoured, and the failure returns to over-reporting. An earlier draft closed this by mandating that `snapshot::write` reconcile; that is not restored, because it would buy a permanently destructive change to a shared writer where one more equality-checked field in an event this design already defines will do.
why: Refuted by F22 on an axis neither I nor the earlier passes had taken: workspace identity. My monotonicity premises are about one workspace's log; the conclusion is about a snapshot's copy versus a workspace's. Nothing binds a memo to its prior renderer, and `snapshot::write` skips a file the current workspace lacks rather than removing it — so rendering M from W2, which never held an ack, leaves W1's ack log beside W2's prose and claims. That is a superset, not a prefix, and it suppresses silently. This is the second time this decision has moved, and it moved on new evidence each time: monotonicity closed the staleness half and left the identity half open. The fix is neither the withdrawn reconciliation nor a change to any shared writer — it is one more component in a key this design already keys on equality.

prop: The acknowledgement is an event in `acks.jsonl` recording the block id, the block's current text, its current citation list, the sha256 digest of each cited claim's proposition **as `claims.jsonl` holds it**, the identity of the workspace minting it, and a verbatim `--why` — plus the `workspace::now_unix()` timestamp every workspace event carries. A listing is suppressed if and only if some ack for that block records a text, citation list and set of cited-claim proposition digests all equal, byte for byte, to the ones the check recomputes for that block at check time, and records a workspace identity equal to the one in the snapshot's `identity.json`. The digests are recomputed from the snapshot's `claims.jsonl` — the same source the ack was minted from, and deliberately not the ledger-derived propositions the in-proof test must use, since the two are not the same string and a claim whose proposition carries an embedded newline or edge whitespace would otherwise be unackable with nothing red to say so. The predicate is pure equality over recomputed values; nothing derived is stored, and no timestamp is compared.
why: C4's repair adds a fourth key component — the minting workspace's identity — and the suppression predicate is stated here, so it has to carry it or the two claims disagree about what the key is.

prop: This design knowingly breaks both halves of TET-30's C11 sentence "Nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes": a tenth file ships, and a new event schema exists. The price is bounded and should be stated rather than absorbed, and it has two components rather than one. The ordinary divergence is that an older build over-reports an entry a newer one suppresses — a difference of one human-owed line, in the safe direction. The sharper one is created by this design's own decision to redden an unreadable acknowledgement log: a single malformed line makes a build carrying that disjunct exit 1 while a build predating the manifest entry never opens the file and exits clean, so the two disagree on the machine partition rather than on a listing. `check` always prints the binary that produced a report, on the stated ground that a report which does not name its build cannot be disbelieved, and that is sufficient to attribute either divergence to its checker — but it is worth being explicit that the second kind is red-versus-green and not merely a line more or less. What the build line does not cover is a reader holding a single old report, with nothing in it to suggest an acknowledgement exists; for them the answer is the log itself, which the snapshot ships beside the memo and which is readable without any tetel build.
why: Qualified: "the only divergence this change can produce" is false once C11 makes an unreadable ack log redden. One malformed line then exits 1 on a build carrying the new disjunct and runs clean on a build predating the manifest entry — a red-versus-green divergence, not an extra human-owed line. The price paragraph priced only the latter.

That shared shape is necessary but not sufficient for the two front ends to agree, and this verb is the case that shows why, in two ways that both concern `text`. First, the ack carries none, yet `ProseParams` declares `text: String` with neither `Option` nor `#[serde(default)]` while `Command::Prose` declares `text: Option<String>`, so an ack over MCP is refused by deserialisation before any `workspace::refuse` is reached while the same ack over the CLI is not; relaxing the MCP field is therefore part of this design, and it moves the create path's missing-text refusal out of the schema into code that must state it. Second, relaxing it is not by itself enough, because on the CLI an absent `--text` does not mean absent: both text-consuming arms resolve it through `resolve_text_or_stdin`, whose `None` case reads stdin, so an ack with no text would block. The ack mode must therefore refuse all six of the other mode-bearing flags outright — `--text`, `--revise`, `--heading`, `--level`, `--cites` and `--before` — and be positioned so it never reaches the stdin fallback. `--level` belongs in that list for a reason worth stating, because it is the member an enumeration written against the MCP shape will miss: on the CLI `--level` is a separate flag consumed only by the heading arm and selected by `--heading`, whereas `ProseParams` folds selector and value into one `heading_level`. Each front end selects its mode with an if/else-if chain that constructs one variant and silently discards whatever inputs that variant has no field for, which is why every one of these refusals must be added rather than inherited: it is the same shape as the defect this crate already fixed once. Of the ack's other refusals only two already exist: a block that does not exist, and an empty `--why` on the identical `why.trim().is_empty()` test that backs "--revise requires --why (revisions must explain themselves)". Three are new gates, because prose creation is deliberately ungated: the block must not be a heading and must carry citations, since a listing exists for neither; and every cited id must resolve to a claim in `claims.jsonl`, because the ack's key is a digest per cited claim and an unresolvable id has none. None inspects the content or plausibility of the reason. The verb cannot refuse an ack on a block that is not currently listed, because an authoring workspace holds no evidence records at all — they live beside the rendered memo — so it cannot compute an anchor; and it need not, since an ack on an unlisted block suppresses nothing.
why: Qualified: my refused-flag list was short by one. `Command::Prose` has seven mode-bearing flags, and `--level` is consumed only by the heading arm while being selected by `--heading` — so an ack arm built to the old list accepts `--level` and silently drops it, the exact defect the claim cites as already fixed once. The MCP shape hides this, since `heading_level` is selector and value at once.
